Subject: Traffic shaping & warm-pool sizing playbook for on‑prem inference

Hi Sara / Acme Ops team,

Thanks for the call earlier — attached is an initial playbook focused on two things we discussed: (1) traffic shaping / queue smoothing to protect p99 latency during bursty customer traffic, and (2) rules for warm‑pool sizing and prefill behavior for your private GPU cluster. The PDF includes our simulation assumptions.

Quick summary of the ask: can you confirm the 30‑day traffic profile we discussed (avg 220 req/s; daily peaks to ~900 req/s; rare spikes up to ~1.4k req/s for 1–3 minutes) and whether your on‑prem NICs support LRO/GRO and 9000 MTU? Those affect the network overhead we budget.

Attachments: redwood-traffic-shaping-playbook.pdf (slides, 18 pages)

High‑level notes in the doc:
- Queue smoothing: leaky‑bucket at the routing layer (global token bucket + per‑customer fairness) + short-term reservoir for quick bursts.
- Warm pool rules: maintain a small hot set of N GPUs with KV‑cache prefill and model replicas bound to NUMA nodes to minimize cold start penalties.
- Scaling policy: predictive scaler keyed off minute-level incoming RPS + 3x short‑term safety cushion and graceful drain during scale‑down.

If you agree I’ll propose concrete sizing numbers (concurrency per GPU, warm‑pool count, burst cushion) and run the sim against your real traffic traces.

Thanks — talk soon.

Sofia Ivanova
Senior Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Traffic shaping & warm-pool sizing playbook for on‑prem inference

Sara — perfect, the trace would be ideal. Based on your constraints I sketched a concrete starting point in the attached CSV sim (warm‑pool‑sim). Key outputs and rationale below.

Attachment: warm-pool-sim-results.csv (csv, 62KB)

Key recommended starting targets (empirical, from sim):
- Sustained throughput target: 500 requests/sec across the private pool (this keeps p50/p90 comfortably within budget).
- Burst guard (short buffer): policy to absorb up to 1.2k req/s for up to 90s using a combination of warm pool headroom + queued reservoir.
- Warm‑pool size: 6 GPUs hot (NUMA pinned replicas) for the model variant tested; i.e., ~1.2x expected working set concurrency plus 2 GPUs headroom during predicted peaks.
- Per‑GPU concurrency: 12 active concurrent requests (model & quantization-specific; derived from your A100 configs).

Traffic‑shaping approach (implementation notes):
1) Global ingress token bucket at the edge limits total accepted RPS to the short‑term cap (1.2k), with a small token refill window (10s) to allow microbursts.
2) Per‑customer fairness: internal weighted queues so a noisy tenant cannot exhaust the reservoir.
3) Request classification: small/cheap vs large/long (token cutoff at 1024) so we apply different concurrency accounting.
4) KV cache prefill: when warm pool spins up, issue background prefill requests using sampled customer prefixes (not full traffic) to warm KV and reduce first‑token latency.

Network and infra notes:
- Enabling 9000 MTU/GRO will reduce CPU interrupt overhead and let you sustain higher RPS per NIC; important if you plan >500 rps/s sustained across many servers.
- Without RDMA we recommend NIC bonding with flow‑pinning and tuning txqueuelen to avoid tail‑lat spikes during egress contention.

Operational protections:
- Circuit breaker at the routing tier: if p99 spikes above target for >30s, start shedding best‑effort requests and fallback to a smaller model variant.
- Graceful drain: scale‑down window of 10min to avoid repeated warming cycles.

Next step: if you share the minute‑level trace I’ll run a more accurate sim and produce a recommended warm‑pool schedule (by hour) and a minute-scale predictive scaler rule.

— Sofia

Subject: Re: Traffic shaping & warm-pool sizing playbook for on‑prem inference

Sofia / team — great direction. A few pragmatic changes from an ops and contractual perspective:

- Bump the sustained target to 600 rps for initial committed SLA (gives Acme a bit more headroom without huge cost). We can still have an enforced short‑term cap at 1.2k for safety but advertise 600 rps as the committed throughput.
- Predictive pre‑warm: use 12h historical windows + recent moving average for next‑hour prediction; if predicted delta > 30% spin up N GPUs proactively.
- Network: insist infra enable 9000 MTU + flow pinning before rollout; otherwise lower per‑GPU concurrency to avoid NIC saturation.
- Add an ingress soft‑queue depth metric to our dashboard (queue length, oldest item age) so SREs can see when smoothing is active.

Operational ask: can we add a short runbook section that lists exact commands for prefill (e.g., curl sequences with header X-Redwood-Warm:1) and a togglable flag to force‑warm pool for testing? I can author that.

Marissa
Director, Customer Solutions | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Traffic shaping & warm-pool sizing playbook for on‑prem inference

Couple of notes on SLA / degradation behavior:

- P99 target: Acme asked for aggressive p99 targets — propose we commit to p99 ≤ 150ms for the committed 600 rps; beyond that (when short‑term cap invoked) we allow best‑effort traffic and aim for graceful degradation.
- Fallbacks: define a fallback model variant and a fast‑path that returns concise responses (truncate long outputs) when circuit breaker trips. That keeps user experience predictable.
- Alerts: create a composite alert that fires when ingress rate > 80% of committed throughput and queue depth > 75% of reservoir capacity for > 45s.
- Testing: run a 2hr soak test with scheduled 90s microbursts at 1.2x and confirm KV prefill reduces first‑token latency by >35% relative to cold starts.

I can draft the SLA language and the fallback model rules if you want.

— Rishi
Head of Product, Dedicated & Private Deployments | Redwood Inference

Thanks everyone — summary and next steps:

Decisions made
- Committed throughput (SLA): 600 rps sustained.
- Short‑term cap for burst protection: 1.2k rps for up to 90s (absorbed by warm pool + reservoir).
- Warm pool initial size: 6 GPUs hot (NUMA pinned replicas) with KV prefill.
- Per‑GPU concurrency: 12 (subject to final sim after we get traces).
- P99 target for committed throughput: ≤ 150ms. Circuit breaker and fallback model variant for best‑effort traffic.

Action items
- Acme (Sara): share minute‑level anonymized trace -> due 2026‑09‑10 EOD.
- Infra (Marissa): enable 9000 MTU + GRO on bonded NICs; leave notes for flow‑pinning -> due 2026‑09‑12.
- Product (Rishi): draft SLA blurb and fallback model rules -> due 2026‑09‑14.
- Ops (Sofia): run detailed sim with provided trace and deliver hour‑by‑hour warm‑pool schedule + Terraform patch for the predictive scaler -> due 2026‑09‑17.

I’ll create JIRA INF-4821 and share the Drive folder with the runbook.

Thanks — will follow up once the trace is in.
